kurals.tamil:
அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போலத் தம்மை
இகழ்வார்ப் பொறுத்தல் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Agazhvaaraith thaangum nilampoalath thammai,
Igazhvaarp poruththal thalai.
kurals.meaning: Just as the earth keeps holding up even the people who dig into it, the highest virtue is to patiently bear with those who insult and belittle us.
kurals.elementary: Think about the ground under your feet. People dig holes in it, stomp on it and poke it with shovels, and it still holds everybody up without complaining. This kural says the best kind of person is like that ground: when someone is mean to you, you stay steady and kind instead of hitting back.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with one of the most famous images in Tamil ethics: the earth (நிலம்) that supports the very people who dig into it (அகழ்வார்). The two verbs are set side by side on purpose. அகழ் (to dig, to wound the ground) matches இகழ் (to scorn, to wound with words), so an insult is pictured as digging into a person, and the patient person takes it in the way soil does, without caving in. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah point out that the earth doesn't just put up with the digger; it keeps holding him up so he doesn't fall, which makes endurance an active kind of support. The last word, தலை ('the foremost'), puts forbearance at the head of the virtues and sets up the thesis the rest of the chapter develops. Other traditions reach for the same metaphor: the Sanskrit kṣamā means both 'earth' and 'forgiveness,' and the Buddha compares abusive speech to a man trying to dig away the whole earth with a hoe.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And because it is seen that there are in the world men who are forgiving like the Earth, it is therefore that creatures derive their life and prosperity.”
hinduism.explanation: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to take revenge on the Kauravas. He refuses, arguing that the world survives only because some people forgive the way the earth does.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the kural's own image: forbearance modeled on the ground, which endures injury and keeps supporting others.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section XXIX (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Explicit earth-as-forgiveness simile. The Sanskrit kṣamā itself means both 'earth' and 'forbearance', which strengthens the parallel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.”
christianity.explanation: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his followers not to strike back when they are hit, and to take the next blow instead of returning it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the earth holding up the one who digs it, the disciple takes the injury without hitting back.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on non-retaliation. It has no earth imagery and doesn't rank patience as the foremost virtue.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace,”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes God's true servants as people who walk gently on the earth and answer rude or ignorant speech with peace instead of insults.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link a humble relationship with the earth to a calm, non-retaliating answer when someone insults you.
islam._accuracy_note: Good thematic match on answering insult with calm. The earth is where they walk, not a simile for endurance as in the kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men that were upon the face of the earth.”
judaism.explanation: Miriam and Aaron have just spoken against Moses (Numbers 12:1-2). He doesn't defend himself, and the Torah praises his meekness above everyone on earth.
judaism.tie_back: Moses quietly bears the people who belittle him, which is the kural's ideal of putting up with those who scorn us.
judaism._accuracy_note: The surrounding verses show Moses being spoken against without replying. This verse praises meekness in general, not forbearance under insult specifically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Suppose that a man were to come along carrying a hoe & a basket, saying, ‘I will make this great earth be without earth.’”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares abusive speech aimed at a trained mind to a man trying to dig away the whole earth with a hoe. He only wears himself out. Monks are told to keep goodwill 'equal to the great earth' whatever others say to them.
buddhism.tie_back: The image is almost the same as the kural's: a digger with a tool against an earth that can't be used up, standing for a patient mind under insult.
buddhism.source: Kakacūpama Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 21 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match. Both use the digger-vs-earth image for patience under abuse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Ulysses stood firm as a rock and the blow did not even stagger him”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus comes home disguised as a beggar, and the suitor Antinous throws a footstool at him. He doesn't flinch or strike back, although Homer adds that he silently thought about revenge.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus stands like rock or earth under the insult and blow, the way the kural's ideal person bears whoever wounds him.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XVII (trans. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The outward endurance matches, but Odysseus is holding back for later revenge, which is unlike the kural's selfless forbearance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius tells himself to be like a headland that the waves keep hitting. It doesn't move, and in the end it calms the water around it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Stoic uses a landform as his model of patience, just as Valluvar uses the earth.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel: a land-feature simile for unshaken endurance. The waves stand for misfortune generally, not insult specifically.

kurals.tamil:
பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் அதனை
மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Poruththal irappinai endrum adhanai,
Maraththal adhaninum nandru.
kurals.meaning: Always bear with wrongs done to you, even ones that go beyond all limits. Forgetting them completely is better still.
kurals.elementary: If a friend breaks your favorite toy, being patient about it is good. This kural says something is even better: letting it go so completely that you stop thinking about it. Holding onto a hurt is like carrying a heavy rock in your pocket, and forgetting it is like finally throwing the rock away.
kurals.university: The couplet sets up two steps: பொறுத்தல் (bearing a wrong) and, higher still, மறத்தல் (forgetting it). The key word இறப்பு here means 'transgression, going beyond bounds.' Traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagan and Mu. Varadarasan read it as an excessive wrong, not as 'death,' although some popular modern glosses take it as 'until death.' Valluvar's point is psychological: if you endure a wrong but still keep a record of it, the endurance is incomplete, because the remembered wrong keeps feeding resentment. Real forbearance lets the grievance go altogether. Rabbinic law draws a similar line between taking vengeance and bearing a grudge (Leviticus 19:18, discussed in Talmud Yoma 23a), and Nietzsche later observed that some strong natures 'forgive' simply by forgetting.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who beareth not malice towards others but is kind to all, who being weak disputeth not with others, who speaketh not arrogantly, and forgeteth a quarrel, is praised everywhere.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura advises King Dhritarashtra that the person everyone praises holds no malice and actually forgets his quarrels instead of keeping them alive.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, it puts forgetting a dispute above merely putting up with it.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIII, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Explicitly praises forgetting a quarrel. It is one item in a list rather than a two-step ranking like the kural's.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; … is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;”
christianity.explanation: Paul says love is long-suffering and 'thinketh no evil.' The Greek phrase (ou logizetai to kakon) means love doesn't keep a record of wrongs done to it.
christianity.tie_back: 'Suffereth long' corresponds to the kural's bearing, and 'thinketh no evil' (not keeping a ledger of injuries) to its forgetting.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers both steps (long-suffering, then not recording the wrong). The 'no record' sense depends on the Greek; the KJV wording is less explicit.

islam.quote_or_event: “and let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allāh should forgive you? And Allāh is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: According to the classical exegetes, this verse was revealed after Abu Bakr swore to stop supporting a relative who had joined in slandering his daughter Aisha. The Qur'an tells him to pardon (ʿafw) and also to overlook (ṣafḥ), that is, to turn the page completely.
islam.tie_back: Pardoning and then overlooking follows the same two steps as the kural's bearing and then forgetting.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong parallel. ṣafḥ (turning away from the matter) is close to 'forgetting'; the occasion of revelation comes from tafsir tradition.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids two separate things: taking revenge, and bearing a grudge. The Talmud (Yoma 23a) explains that even helping someone while reminding them of their past wrong counts as bearing a grudge.
judaism.tie_back: Not taking vengeance matches the kural's bearing; not bearing a grudge, not even keeping the memory alive, matches its forgetting.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close conceptual match, especially read with the Talmud's vengeance/grudge distinction (explanation only, not quoted).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who do not harbor such thoughts still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's opening verses teach that hatred ends only when we stop going over the wrongs done to us.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the kural's 'forgetting': letting go of the memory of the injury so it no longer controls the mind.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct match on letting go of the remembered wrong as the higher path.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Ajax, will you not forget and forgive even in death, but must the judgement about that hateful armour still rankle with you?”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Underworld, Odysseus meets the ghost of Ajax, who is still furious about losing the armour of Achilles to him. Odysseus begs him to forget. Ajax turns away without a word.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the kural: a grievance held even past death shows what refusing to forget costs.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XI (trans. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A counter-example rather than a parallel. It shows the failure to forget that the kural warns against.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Mirabeau, who had no memory for any insults and meannesses which were practised on him, and who was only incapable of forgiving because he forgot.”
philosophy.explanation: Nietzsche praises strong natures who can't take their enemies' offences seriously for long. His example is Mirabeau, who didn't need to forgive because he simply forgot.
philosophy.tie_back: Nietzsche arrives at the kural's conclusion, that forgetting a wrong goes beyond forgiving it, though for a different reason.
philosophy.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Genealogy of Morals, First Essay, §10 (trans. Horace B. Samuel)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Striking match on 'forgetting above forgiving.' Nietzsche frames it as a trait of strong natures rather than a moral duty.

kurals.tamil:
இன்மையுள் இன்மை விருந்தொரால் வன்மையுள்
வன்மை மடவார்ப் பொறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Inmaiyul inmai virundhoraal vanmaiyul,
Vanmai madavaarp porai.
kurals.meaning: The worst poverty of all is being unable to welcome a guest, and the greatest strength of all is patiently putting up with foolish people.
kurals.elementary: Being poor isn't only about having little money. This kural says the saddest kind of poor is not being able to share even a snack with a friend who visits. Being strong isn't only about big muscles either: the strongest kind of strong is staying calm when someone acts silly or rude to you.
kurals.university: Valluvar builds the couplet on a double superlative, இன்மையுள் இன்மை ('the poverty within poverty') and வன்மையுள் வன்மை ('the strength within strength'), and uses it to pair two virtues that seem unrelated. The first half looks back to the chapter on hospitality (விருந்தோம்பல், ch. 9), where turning away a guest is the gravest failure of a household. The second half redefines might as the ability to bear the provocations of மடவார், 'the ignorant' or 'foolish.' Setting them side by side suggests a shared logic: hospitality and forbearance both measure inner abundance, not outward resources. Redefining strength as self-mastery is one of the most widely shared moral reversals across traditions, from the Mishnah's 'Who is mighty?' to the hadith about the strong man who controls his anger.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “These two, O king, live (as it were) in a region higher than heaven itself, viz., a man of power endued with forgiveness, and poor man that is charitable.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura names two people who stand above heaven itself: a powerful man who forgives, and a poor man who still gives.
hinduism.tie_back: It pairs the same two ideas as the kural, generosity in poverty and forbearance in power, in one saying.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIII, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Remarkable structural match that links poverty/giving with strength/forgiveness. It praises the positive ideal rather than naming the worst poverty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy that a servant of God must not quarrel but stay gentle and patient. The next verse applies this to people who oppose him and need instruction.
christianity.tie_back: Being patient and gentle with the contentious and unteaching is the kural's 'strength of strengths,' bearing with the foolish.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches patience with difficult people. It doesn't cast this as strength and has nothing on hospitality.

islam.quote_or_event: “The strong is not the one who overcomes the people by his strength, but the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines strength: the truly strong person is not the wrestler who throws others down but the one who masters himself when provoked.
islam.tie_back: This is the kural's 'strength within strength' exactly: real power is holding back, not fighting.
islam._accuracy_note: Near-direct match on redefining strength as self-restraint. It doesn't mention fools or hospitality.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma's famous teaching redefines might as control over one's own impulses, and backs it with the proverb that the slow-to-anger outrank warriors.
judaism.tie_back: The same reversal as the kural: the greatest strength is restraint in the face of provocation.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on the 'true might' reversal. The companion clause 'Who is rich?' is about contentment, not hospitality.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who without resentment endures abuse, beating and punishment; whose power, real might, is patience — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the true holy man as someone whose real power is patience under abuse.
buddhism.tie_back: 'Real might is patience' is almost a translation of the kural's வன்மையுள் வன்மை ... பொறை.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the second half ('patience is real might').

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as travelers, are turned away from a thousand wealthy homes. The poor old couple Baucis and Philemon welcome them and share the little food they have.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid's tale the gods reward the poor couple's hospitality and punish the stingy neighbors. However poor they were, Baucis and Philemon never fell into the 'poverty' of refusing a guest.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It illustrates the kural's first half: the real poverty is being unable to welcome a guest, not a lack of means.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VIII (Baucis and Philemon)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Covers only the hospitality half. There is no strong Greek myth about bearing fools as 'true strength'.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius starts each day expecting to meet difficult people, and reminds himself that their faults come from ignorance, so he shouldn't be angry with them.
philosophy.tie_back: Bearing with the foolish (மடவார்) because they are ignorant is the kural's picture of real strength.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on patiently bearing the ignorant. It doesn't call this strength or mention hospitality.

kurals.tamil:
நிறையுடைமை நீங்காமை வேண்டின் பொறையுடைமை
போற்றி யொழுகப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Niraiyudaimai neengaamai vendin poraiyudaimai,
Potri yozhugap padum.
kurals.meaning: If you never want to lose your fullness of character, your inner completeness and self-possession, you must cherish patience and live by it.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your good character is a glass filled to the top with water. Every time you lose your temper, some spills out. This kural says that if you want to keep your glass full, you have to carry it carefully, which means being patient all the time.
kurals.university: நிறை is a rich Tamil word meaning fullness, completeness, and also self-restraint or integrity. It describes a wife's guarded constancy in chapter 6 and the sages 'full of word' in chapter 3. Valluvar makes பொறையுடைமை (possessing patience) the precondition for keeping நிறையுடைமை (possessing fullness). The two '-உடைமை' compounds deliberately echo each other, which suggests patience is not one virtue among many but the container that keeps the others from leaking away. The phrase போற்றி ஒழுகுதல் ('to guard and live by') implies constant vigilance, not occasional restraint, and Solomon Pappaiah reads நிறை as சான்றாண்மை, the complete nobility of character treated in chapter 99. The Epistle of James makes almost the same claim, that patience is what makes a person 'perfect and entire.'

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is equal to friends and enemies, who is equipoised in honor and dishonor, heat and cold, happiness and distress, fame and infamy, who is always free from contaminating association, always silent and satisfied with anything, who doesn’t care for any residence, who is fixed in knowledge and who is engaged in devotional service – such a person is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as someone whose mind stays whole and steady (sthira-matiḥ) through honor and dishonor, praise and blame.
hinduism.tie_back: An even mind under insult or praise is the kind of unbroken inner fullness (நிறை) that the kural says patience protects.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches steadiness under dishonor. It doesn't explicitly say that patience preserves one's completeness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that patience, allowed to do its full work, makes a believer complete and lacking nothing.
christianity.tie_back: 'Perfect and entire, wanting nothing' is almost a definition of நிறை, and both texts make patience its source.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: patience leads to completeness/fullness.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allāh is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents patience (ṣabr) as one of the two supports of the believer's life, together with prayer.
islam.tie_back: Both treat patience as something you must keep hold of to stay upright and whole.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of patience as a foundation. It doesn't say patience preserves one's integrity or completeness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth;”
judaism.explanation: Among the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, God is erech apayim, 'long-suffering.' Rabbinic tradition teaches imitation of God: as He is merciful and patient, so should you be.
judaism.tie_back: Patience is part of the divine fullness of character. To keep that completeness in yourself, you have to practise long-suffering too.
judaism._accuracy_note: Patience as an attribute of perfect character. The link to keeping one's own completeness comes through the rabbinic idea of imitatio Dei, which is interpretive.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “a monk may be ever so gentle, ever so mild-tempered, ever so calm, as long as he is not touched by disagreeable aspects of speech. But it is only when disagreeable aspects of speech touch him that he can truly be known as gentle, mild-tempered, & calm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells of Lady Vedehikā, famous for her gentleness, who lost that reputation the moment her maid tested her patience. Good character that can't bear provocation was never really secure.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the kural's warning: without patience, your fullness of character leaks away the moment it is tested.
buddhism.source: Kakacūpama Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 21 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match: patience under provocation is what keeps a good character intact.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “at night she would unpick the stitches again by torchlight. She fooled us in this way for three years without our finding it out”
greek_mythology.explanation: For years Penelope endures the pressure of the arrogant suitors. She patiently weaves Laertes' shroud by day and unravels it by night, so that she keeps her faithfulness to Odysseus intact.
greek_mythology.tie_back: நிறை also means constancy and chastity. Penelope's patient endurance is what keeps her integrity from being lost.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XXIV (trans. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit for the 'constancy' sense of நிறை. Penelope's patience is strategic and aimed at suitors, not a response to personal insult.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you hear unpleasant language, you will find patience.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that for every hard thing we have a matching inner capacity. For insulting words, that capacity is patience, and using it keeps us from being 'hurried away' by events.
philosophy.tie_back: Keeping patience at the ready protects the self-possession that the kural calls நிறை.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match: patience as the faculty that preserves self-command. It doesn't use the language of 'fullness'.

kurals.tamil:
ஒறுத்தாரை ஒன்றாக வையாரே வைப்பர்
பொறுத்தாரைப் பொன்போற் பொதிந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Oruththaarai ondraaga vaiyaare vaippar,
Poruththaaraip ponpor podhindhu.
kurals.meaning: People count those who punish every wrong done to them as worth nothing. Those who forbear they treasure, keeping them close like wrapped-up gold.
kurals.elementary: Two kids get pushed in the lunch line. One shoves back hard, and the other says, 'It's okay.' Later, which one do people trust and want as a friend? This kural says people treasure the patient one like a piece of gold kept safe in a box, while the one who always hits back isn't valued at all.
kurals.university: ஒறுத்தார் ('those who punished' the offender) and பொறுத்தார் ('those who bore it') differ by a single initial consonant, and Valluvar uses the near-rhyme to make the moral contrast audible. ஒன்றாக வையார் means such people are not counted as anything at all, while பொன்போற் பொதிந்து வைப்பர் ('they wrap and keep like gold') suggests a treasure bundled up and stored with care. The judgement is a social one: honor goes not to the person who wins the exchange of blows but to the one who refuses it. That reverses a warrior-culture instinct that leaving a slight unavenged is shameful. Aristotle is a useful contrast: he praises the good-tempered man who 'tends to make allowances,' but warns that putting up with every insult can look 'slavish.' Valluvar settles that tension firmly on the side of forbearance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Forgiveness is a virtue of the weak, and an ornament of the strong.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura admits that people sometimes mistake the forgiving for weak, but insists that forgiveness is great power, a jewel worn by the strong.
hinduism.tie_back: 'Ornament' matches the kural's gold. The forbearing person is prized and adorned, not despised.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIII, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good match on forbearance as a precious ornament. It doesn't explicitly contrast this with how the vengeful are regarded.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers that the real glory is patiently enduring mistreatment you didn't deserve.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say where true honor lies: with the one who bears wrong patiently, not the one who hits back.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches honor for patient endurance. The esteem here is God's, whereas the kural's is society's.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whoever is patient and forgives - indeed, that is of the matters [worthy] of resolve.”
islam.explanation: Right after allowing proportionate retaliation, the Qur'an praises patience and forgiveness as a higher, more resolute path.
islam.tie_back: Both texts rank the one who forbears above the one who retaliates.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on ranking forbearance above retaliation. It lacks the kural's image of social esteem ('like gold').

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is the discretion of a man to be slow to anger, And it is his glory to pass over a transgression.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs calls overlooking an offence a person's glory, that is, their honor and splendor.
judaism.tie_back: 'His glory' corresponds to the kural's 'treasured like gold': forbearance is what earns honor.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match: forbearance brings glory or esteem.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who can blame such a one, as worthy as a coin of refined gold? Even the gods praise him; by Brahma, too, is he praised.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Dhammapada's chapter on anger, the self-controlled person of flawless character is called as precious as refined gold and praised even by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: It uses the same gold image as the kural for the person who has mastered anger.
buddhism._accuracy_note: The gold simile matches, and the verse sits in the Anger chapter. Its subject is flawless character in general, not forbearance specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles, insulted when Agamemnon takes his prize Briseis, withdraws from the war in rage. His unappeased anger brings countless deaths on the Greeks.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad opens by naming Achilles' wrath as its subject, and it shows that refusing to let an insult pass wins the hero no lasting honor, only grief for his friends and for himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A counter-example: the person who must avenge every slight ends up diminished, not treasured.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Book I (trans. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates the vengeful half by contrast. Greek heroic culture generally honored retaliation, so no close positive parallel exists.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the good-tempered man is not revengeful, but rather tends to make allowances.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says good temper is praised, and that the good-tempered man is not vengeful but makes allowances. He also warns that tolerating every insult can look 'slavish.'
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle praises the forbearing over the revengeful, as the kural does, though with more reservations.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Praises the non-vengeful, but Aristotle also counts some anger as a virtue, which sets him against the kural's stronger position.

kurals.tamil:
ஒறுத்தார்க்கு ஒருநாளை இன்பம் பொறுத்தார்க்குப்
பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oruththaarkku orunaalai inbam poruththaarkkup,
Pondrun thunaiyum pugazh.
kurals.meaning: People who take revenge enjoy a pleasure that lasts a single day. People who forbear win a fame that lasts until the world itself passes away.
kurals.elementary: Getting back at someone can feel good, for about one day. Then the good feeling is gone. Being the person who stayed kind is different: people remember it and talk about it for a very, very long time.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two time-scales against each other: ஒருநாளை இன்பம் ('one day's pleasure') and பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ் ('fame until [the world] perishes'). Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah read பொன்றும் as the ending of the world, while Kalaignar reads it as 'throughout one's life.' Either way the basic contrast between passing gratification and lasting reputation holds. Valluvar is speaking the language of புகழ், the enduring renown he devotes chapter 24 to, where reputation is treated as the only thing that outlives the body. The psychological point is sharp: Aristotle also observes that revenge 'relieves' anger by 'producing ... pleasure instead of pain,' but Valluvar insists that this pleasure is the shortest-lived of goods.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man may attain renown in this world by doing two things, viz., by refraining from harsh speech, and by disregarding those that are wicked.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura names renown as the reward for not answering harshly and for disregarding the provocations of the wicked.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, it makes lasting fame the fruit of forbearance.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIII, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct match on 'forbearance brings renown'. It lacks the contrast with revenge's brief pleasure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.”
christianity.explanation: James points to Job, whose patience became proverbial and is still remembered long after his trials ended.
christianity.tie_back: Job's lasting fame for endurance illustrates the kural's claim that praise for the patient outlives them.
christianity._accuracy_note: Job's enduring renown fits well. There is no explicit contrast with revenge.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account [i.e., limit].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an promises the patient a reward so large it can't be measured.
islam.tie_back: The unlimited reward of the patient matches the kural's everlasting praise, set against revenge's one day.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on a limitless reward for patience. The reward is divine, not worldly fame.

judaism.quote_or_event: “whoever forgoes his reckonings with others for injustices done to him, the heavenly court in turn forgoes punishment for all his sins”
judaism.explanation: Rava teaches that a person who lets injustices against him pass is himself treated with lasting divine mercy.
judaism.tie_back: Forgoing retaliation brings a lasting reward, while insisting on your due brings nothing that endures.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Rosh Hashanah 17a (William Davidson/Koren translation)
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the lasting reward for forbearance. The reward is divine forgiveness rather than worldly fame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that returning hatred never brings lasting peace, and that only non-hatred does so, as an eternal law.
buddhism.tie_back: Revenge brings only a short relief, while forbearance produces something lasting, which is the kural's contrast.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches 'retaliation doesn't last, forbearance does'. It speaks of peace rather than fame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The fame, therefore, of her virtue shall never die, and the immortals shall compose a song that shall be welcome to all mankind in honour of the constancy of Penelope.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Underworld, Agamemnon's ghost declares that Penelope's patient faithfulness through twenty years of pressure will be famous forever.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Patient endurance wins undying fame, just as the kural promises praise until the world ends.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XXIV (trans. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on 'endurance brings deathless fame'. Penelope's patience is constancy rather than forbearance of personal insult.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For remember that, if you adhere to the same point, those very persons who at first ridiculed will afterwards admire you.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the new philosopher to expect mockery and to bear it without replying, because steady endurance eventually turns ridicule into admiration.
philosophy.tie_back: Enduring insult earns lasting esteem, while retaliating would forfeit it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches forbearance leading to esteem. The scope is smaller than the kural's world-long fame.

kurals.tamil:
திறனல்ல தற்பிறர் செய்யினும் நோநொந்து
அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thiranalla tharpirar seyyinum nononthu,
Aranalla seyyaamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: Even when others do you harm you never deserved, it is good to feel sorry for the suffering their wrongdoing will bring on them, and not to do anything unrighteous in return.
kurals.elementary: When someone is unfair to you, you might want to be unfair back. This kural says don't. Instead, feel a little sad for them, because doing wrong usually comes back to hurt the person who does it, and keep doing the right thing yourself.
kurals.university: The key phrase is நோநொந்து. Mu. Varadarasan reads it as grieving over the suffering (நோ) that will fall on the wrongdoer as the fruit of his act, which makes the couplet an ethic of compassion toward the offender rather than mere self-restraint. Solomon Pappaiah offers a slightly different nuance, grieving at the thought that retaliation would hurt him, but both readings end in refusing அறனல்ல, 'what is not dharma.' The couplet therefore goes beyond tolerance to a positive moral stance: being injured doesn't license you to abandon virtue. Socrates states the same principle in the Crito, that it is never right to return wrong for wrong, and Jesus acts it out on the cross by praying for those who crucify him.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which is antagonistic to one's own self, should never be applied in respect of another. Briefly even this is virtue.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura sums up dharma in one rule: never do to another what you would find hurtful yourself.
hinduism.tie_back: Because you know how injury feels, you refuse to inflict it back even when you've been wronged, which is the kural's refusal of 'what is not dharma'.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIX, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A golden-rule principle that rules out retaliation. It isn't framed specifically around responding to injury or pitying the offender.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
christianity.explanation: While being crucified, Jesus prays for his executioners and feels for their spiritual danger instead of cursing them.
christianity.tie_back: Grieving for the wrongdoer instead of retaliating is exactly the kural's நோநொந்து.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on compassion for the offender while suffering harm.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the retribution for an evil act is an evil one like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation - his reward is [due] from Allāh. Indeed, He does not like wrongdoers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an allows equal retribution but holds up pardon and reconciliation as the better way, rewarded by God.
islam.tie_back: Both texts steer the injured person away from answering wrong with wrong.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on preferring pardon. The Qur'an permits proportional retaliation, whereas the kural rules out any unrighteous response.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘I will do so to him as he hath done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.’”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs explicitly forbids the tit-for-tat reasoning of paying someone back for what he did to you.
judaism.tie_back: This is the kural's அறனல்ல செய்யாமை: don't answer wrong with wrong.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct match on refusing retaliation. It lacks the kural's compassion for the offender.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever returns insult to one who is insulting, returns taunts to one who is taunting, returns a berating to one who is berating, is said to be eating together, sharing company, with that person.”
buddhism.explanation: When the brahman Akkosaka abuses him, the Buddha refuses the 'meal' of insults, explaining that anyone who returns abuse joins in the offender's wrongdoing.
buddhism.tie_back: Returning wrong for wrong makes you a partner in it, which is why the kural says not to act against dharma even when wronged.
buddhism.source: Akkosa Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.2 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on refusing to reciprocate. The compassion element appears later in the sutta's verses.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Old King Priam comes to Achilles' tent to beg for the body of his son Hector. Achilles, who killed Hector and has been abusing his corpse, is moved by Priam, weeps with him, and returns the body.
greek_mythology.explanation: At the end of the Iliad, Achilles finally feels for his enemy's grief and stops trying to punish him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Feeling for the enemy's suffering instead of continuing to strike at him reflects the kural's நோநொந்து.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Book XXIV (trans. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Here Achilles is the aggressor who relents, not a victim who forbears, so the parallel is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: In prison awaiting execution, Socrates refuses to escape unjustly and states that wronging someone in return is never right, however badly you've been treated.
philosophy.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the kural: however unfitting the harm received, do nothing unrighteous in return.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on non-retaliation. It lacks the kural's pity for the wrongdoer.

kurals.tamil:
மிகுதியான் மிக்கவை செய்தாரைத் தாந்தம்
தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Migudhiyaan mikkavai seydhaaraith thaandham,
Thagudhiyaan vendru vidal.
kurals.meaning: When people swollen with arrogance heap outrageous wrongs on you, defeat them through your own worth, that is, through your patience.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a bully acts big and mean, and you might think the only way to win is to be even meaner. This kural says you can beat them another way: by staying calm and good. Your patience works like a superpower that makes their meanness look small.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on மிகுதி ('excess, arrogance') and தகுதி ('fitness, worth'). The aggressor acts out of surplus (மிகுதியான் மிக்கவை, 'excessive deeds out of excess'), and is to be overcome by the victim's own proper measure (தாந்தம் தகுதியான்). Commentators consistently identify this தகுதி with பொறை, patience itself, so forbearance becomes a strategy for victory rather than passive defeat. The verb, வென்று விடல் ('conquer'), is deliberately martial: Valluvar claims the vocabulary of winning for the person who doesn't retaliate. The same logic appears in Paul's 'overcome evil with good,' in the Qur'an's 'repel evil with what is better,' and in Vidura's maxim that anger is conquered by forgiveness, a maxim that reappears almost word for word in the Dhammapada (v. 223).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Anger must be conquered by forgiveness; and the wicked must be conquered by honesty; the miser must be conquered by liberality, and falsehood must be conquered by truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura teaches that each vice is defeated by its opposite virtue, and anger above all by forgiveness.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the kural, the aggressor is 'conquered' not by force but by one's own virtue of forbearance.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIX, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match. It shares the 'conquer by virtue' framing and verb.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul closes his teaching on non-retaliation by telling believers to defeat evil by doing good, not by answering in kind.
christianity.tie_back: The same reversal of victory: the wronged person wins through goodness, not counter-attack.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on 'conquer wrong through one's own goodness'.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon, the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells believers to push back evil with something better, and promises that this can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: Repelling the aggressor with better conduct is the kural's victory through one's own worth.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match. It even adds the enemy-to-friend outcome.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Others say: [Who is mighty?] Who turns an enemy into his friend.”
judaism.explanation: Expanding Ben Zoma's 'Who is mighty?', Avot de-Rabbi Natan records the view that the mightiest person is the one who wins over his enemy and makes him a friend.
judaism.tie_back: Victory through character rather than force is the kural's 'conquer them by your own worth'.
judaism.source: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 23:1 (trans. A. Cohen, Soncino)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on redefining victory. It doesn't specify patience as the means.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that every kind of wrongdoer is defeated by the opposite virtue, the angry by non-anger.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the kural's teaching exactly: conquer the aggressor with your own virtue. It also echoes Vidura's Mahabharata maxim almost word for word.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on 'overcome by one's own virtue'.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus' Eumenides, the raging Furies threaten to poison Athens after Orestes is acquitted. Athena doesn't fight them. She calms them with patient persuasion and offers them honor, until they become the 'Kindly Ones.'
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena wins over the enraged goddesses through patience and persuasion (Peitho), not force, and turns them from enemies into protectors.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Overcoming aggressors through one's own character rather than retaliation is the kural's victory by தகுதி.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Good match on victory by patient persuasion, but Athena is not the injured party.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that a person who lives by reason tries, as far as possible, to repay others' hatred, anger and contempt with love and generosity, because hatred grows when returned and can be destroyed by love.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, answering hostility with love is not weakness but the rational way to defeat hatred.
philosophy.tie_back: Defeating the aggressor through one's own better disposition is the kural's தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Proposition 46 and proof
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase (not verified verbatim). Strong conceptual match on overcoming hostility through virtue.

kurals.tamil:
துறந்தாரின் தூய்மை உடையர் இறந்தார்வாய்
இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற் பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thurandhaarin thooimai udaiyar irandhaarvaai,
Innaachchol norkir pavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who can patiently bear the harsh words of people who overstep every limit are as pure as those who have renounced the world.
kurals.elementary: Monks and nuns who give up everything are often thought of as very pure. This kural says you don't have to leave home to be that pure. If someone yells nasty words at you and you stay calm, your heart is just as clean as theirs.
kurals.university: இறந்தார் here doesn't mean 'the dead.' It means 'those who have transgressed' (from இற, to go beyond), the same root as இறப்பு in Kural 152. Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar confirm this sense, though some popular glosses take it literally. The comparison with துறந்தார் ('renunciants') matters because these chapters belong to இல்லறவியல், the section on the householder's life: Valluvar claims that a householder who endures insult reaches the purity normally reserved for ascetics. Solomon Pappaiah makes this explicit, saying that even living a household life, such a person is as pure as a renunciant. The verb நோற்றல் ('to endure as an austerity') anticipates the next couplet's comparison with fasting and recasts patience itself as a form of tapas.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him patiently bear hard words, let him not insult anybody, and let him not become anybody's enemy for the sake of this (perishable) body. Against an angry man let him not in return show anger, let him bless when he is cursed”
hinduism.explanation: Among the rules for the wandering renunciant (sannyāsin), Manu requires him to bear harsh words patiently and to bless those who curse him.
hinduism.tie_back: Bearing harsh words is a defining discipline of the renunciant. The kural says a householder who does the same is equally pure.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match. It shows that enduring harsh words was literally the renunciant's rule, which is the benchmark the kural invokes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:”
christianity.explanation: Peter holds up Christ, who did not answer insult with insult, as the model of holy conduct under abuse.
christianity.tie_back: Bearing abusive words without answering is the mark of the purest life, as in the kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on bearing verbal abuse as a sign of holiness. There is no explicit comparison with ascetics.

islam.quote_or_event: “You will surely be tested in your possessions and in yourselves. And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with Allāh much abuse. But if you are patient and fear Allāh - indeed, that is of the matters [worthy] of resolve.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns believers that they will hear much hurtful speech, and says that patience with it, joined with God-consciousness, is a mark of true resolve.
islam.tie_back: Enduring hurtful words (இன்னாச்சொல்) is treated as a high spiritual achievement, as in the kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct match on patiently bearing abusive speech. The comparison with ascetic purity is absent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “About those who are insulted and do not insult, who hear their shame and do not respond, who act out of love and are joyful in suffering, the verse says: ‘And they that love Him are as the sun going forth in its might’ (Judges 5:31).”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud praises those who hear themselves shamed without answering, comparing them to the radiant rising sun.
judaism.tie_back: Shining like the sun, the silent bearer of insult has a purity like the kural's renunciant.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match on silent endurance of insult as spiritual greatness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as when people throw what is clean or unclean on the earth — feces, urine, saliva, pus, or blood — the earth is not horrified, humiliated, or disgusted by it”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches the young monk Rahula to make his mind like the earth, which isn't defiled by whatever filth is thrown on it.
buddhism.tie_back: A mind that foul words can't stain is the renunciant's purity the kural describes.
buddhism.source: Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 62 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on purity unaffected by what is 'thrown'. The teaching concerns sense impressions generally, not only speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “he resolved, however, to endure it and keep himself in check”
greek_mythology.explanation: On the road home, the goatherd Melanthius reviles the disguised Odysseus with outrageous language and kicks him. Odysseus considers striking back but chooses to endure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Bearing the insolent words of a man who overstepped all bounds reflects the kural's இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்றல்.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XVII (trans. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear case of enduring insolent speech. Odysseus' restraint is tactical, and there is no link to purity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Remember, that not he who gives ill language or a blow insults, but the principle which represents these things as insulting.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that harsh words have power over us only if we accept them as injuries. The disciplined mind stays untouched.
philosophy.tie_back: A mind that insulting words can't stain has the inner purity the kural credits to those who bear harsh speech.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on inner inviolability under insult. It isn't framed as purity or asceticism.

kurals.tamil:
உண்ணாது நோற்பார் பெரியர் பிறர்சொல்லும்
இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பாரின் பின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Unnaadhu norpaar periyar pirarsollum,
Innaachchol norpaarin pin.
kurals.meaning: Those who fast and endure hunger are great, but they rank only after those who endure the cruel words other people speak to them.
kurals.elementary: Going without food for a whole day to be good is really hard, and people admire it. This kural says something is even harder and better: when someone says mean things to you and you swallow your anger and stay kind, you are the real champion.
kurals.university: Valluvar closes the chapter by ranking two kinds of நோன்பு (austerity): உண்ணாது நோற்றல், enduring hunger by fasting, and இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்றல், enduring cruel speech. By placing the faster 'after' (பின்) the one who bears insult, he puts the most visible ascetic practice of his time, prominent in both Jain and Brahmanical asceticism, below an inner, social virtue. Repeating நோற்பார் in both lines insists that patience is itself tapas, completing the argument begun in Kural 159. The ranking resonates with the Dhammapada's 'Enduring patience is the highest austerity,' with the hadith that tells a fasting person to answer abuse by saying 'I am fasting,' and with Isaiah's prophetic critique that a true fast is measured by ethical conduct.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “forgiveness is stored ascetic merit; forgiveness protecteth the ascetic merit of the future; forgiveness is asceticism; forgiveness is holiness”
hinduism.explanation: In the verses Yudhishthira attributes to the sage Kashyapa, forgiveness is declared to be asceticism (tapas) itself and the guardian of all ascetic merit.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, it counts forbearance as the true austerity, above physical penances.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section XXIX (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match: forbearance equated with tapas. It doesn't explicitly rank it above fasting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus pronounces those who are reviled and slandered 'blessed.' In the same sermon (Matthew 6:16-18) he warns that fasting done for show has no value.
christianity.tie_back: Enduring others' evil words is blessed, while external fasting is played down, which comes close to the kural's ranking.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches blessedness for bearing insult. The ranking against fasting is only implicit in the wider Sermon on the Mount.

islam.quote_or_event: “Fasting is a shield (or a screen or a shelter). So, the person observing fasting should avoid sexual relation with his wife and should not behave foolishly and impudently, and if somebody fights with him or abuses him, he should tell him twice, 'I am fasting.'”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that a fast is only complete if the faster also refuses to return abuse. Bearing insult is part of the fast's real substance.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link fasting and enduring abusive speech, and make patience under insult the deeper discipline.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match: it joins fasting and bearing abuse. It subordinates rather than strictly ranks.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Is not this the fast that I have chosen? To loose the fetters of wickedness, To undo the bands of the yoke, And to let the oppressed go free, And that ye break every yoke?”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah rebukes people who fast while behaving badly. God values ethical conduct above abstaining from food.
judaism.tie_back: Like the kural, it ranks moral virtue above fasting as the true austerity.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on 'ethics outranks fasting'. The ethic here is justice, not patience under insult.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Enduring patience is the highest austerity. ‘Nibbana is supreme,’ say the Buddhas. He is not a true monk who harms another, nor a true renunciate who oppresses others.”
buddhism.explanation: In the verses known as the Ovāda Pātimokkha, the Buddhas declare patient endurance (khanti) the supreme form of tapas.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a direct statement of the kural: patient endurance ranks above every other austerity, fasting included.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: patience as the highest austerity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He endured both being struck and insulted without a word, though he was in his own house”
greek_mythology.explanation: The dead suitor Amphimedon recalls how the disguised Odysseus, a starving beggar in his own hall, silently bore their blows and insults.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus endures hunger and insult together, and Homer presents his silent endurance of abuse as his greatest test.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XXIV (trans. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Combines hunger and bearing insult. There is no explicit ranking, and the endurance serves a plan of revenge.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for the most part he was despised and laughed at, yet bore all this ill-usage patiently.”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes Laertius reports that Socrates was famous for plain living and endurance of hunger and cold, but even more for calmly bearing mockery and abuse, including Xanthippe's scolding.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates combines bodily austerity with patience under insult, and it is the patience his biographer dwells on, much as the kural ranks it higher.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers II.21 (trans. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on patient endurance of abuse, with bodily austerity described nearby (II.27). There is no formal ranking.
